lead: This unit explains how chemical energy becomes electrical energy in cells, batteries, fuel cells and supercapacitors, and how the same electrochemistry makes metals corrode. After it you can calculate electrode potentials and EMF, choose a reference electrode, compare battery performance, and select cathodic protection or a coating for a corroding structure.
about: The unit starts with galvanic cells and single electrode potentials in 4.1. Chapter 4.2 adds the Nernst equation, free energy and EMF, and 4.3 explains calomel and glass reference electrodes. Chapter 4.4 uses these ideas in potentiometry and electrolyte conductance. Chapters 4.5 and 4.6 compare primary and secondary batteries, then open up lead-acid and lithium-ion cells. Chapter 4.7 extends the same electrode reactions to fuel cells and supercapacitors. The last two chapters turn the chemistry around: 4.8 explains electrochemical corrosion, the galvanic series and the factors that speed it up, and 4.9 shows how cathodic protection and coatings stop it.

chapters.idea: A cell is two half-cells, and each half-cell has an electrode potential set by its redox couple; the cell EMF is cathode potential minus anode potential.
chapters.depth: Galvanic or voltaic cell, Daniell cell, salt bridge, anode oxidation and cathode reduction, cell notation. Single electrode potential, standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) with E° = 0.00 V by convention, standard conditions 298 K, 1 bar, 1 M. Standard electrode potentials and the electrochemical series. Use E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Some syllabi call this a galvanic cell or voltaic cell.

figure.title: Daniell cell
figure.aria: A zinc electrode in zinc ion solution connects through a salt bridge to copper ion solution and a copper electrode.

chapters.example: For the Daniell cell Zn | Zn²⁺ (1 M) || Cu²⁺ (1 M) | Cu, E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. Find E°cell. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
chapters.trap: Do not add the two electrode potentials with their signs and then forget the anode sign. Use E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; the zinc electrode is −0.76 V, not +0.76 V.
chapters.prereq: School-level redox and oxidation number; Unit 1 coordination compounds helps with oxidation states.
chapters.leave: Concentration dependence and the Nernst equation to 4.2; reference electrodes to 4.3; battery applications to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Electrode potential changes with concentration through the Nernst equation, and cell EMF is tied to Gibbs free energy by ΔG = −nFE.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at full thermodynamic depth. Nernst equation E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q; at 298 K, E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. Define R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T in kelvin, n electrons, F = 96485 C mol⁻¹, Q reaction quotient. ΔG = −nFE, ΔG° = −nFE°, ΔG° = −RT ln K, and E° = (0.0592/n) log K at 298 K. Expressions for metal/metal-ion, gas and redox electrodes. Brief ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and temperature coefficient if taught.

figure.aria: A straight line falls as log Q increases, showing the Nernst equation for a two-electron cell with E° equal to 1.10 V.

chapters.trap: Use log base 10 with 0.0592, not ln, and put products over reactants in Q. Also n is the number of electrons in the balanced cell reaction, not the charge on one ion.
chapters.prereq: 4.1; Unit 3 thermodynamics for Gibbs free energy and equilibrium.
chapters.leave: pH measurement and potentiometric titrations to 4.4; battery and fuel-cell applications to 4.5–4.7.

chapters.idea: A reference electrode gives a stable known potential; calomel uses Hg/Hg₂Cl₂ and glass uses a pH-sensitive glass membrane.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail. Saturated calomel electrode (SCE): Hg pool, Hg₂Cl₂ paste, saturated KCl, porous plug; half-reaction Hg₂Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Hg + 2Cl⁻; SCE potential about +0.241 V vs SHE at 25 °C. Glass electrode: thin glass bulb, internal 0.1 M HCl and Ag/AgCl wire; measured cell EMF changes by about 0.0592 V per pH unit at 298 K. Applications: pH measurement and as reference in potentiometry. Some syllabi call these secondary reference electrodes.

figure.aria: A tree splits reference electrodes into calomel, with mercury paste, potassium chloride and a porous plug, and glass, with a glass membrane, internal acid and silver-silver chloride wire.

chapters.example: A saturated calomel electrode has E = +0.241 V vs SHE. It is coupled with a copper electrode in 1 M Cu²⁺, and copper is the cathode. The voltmeter reads 0.099 V. Find E(Cu). E(Cu) = 0.099 + 0.241 = 0.340 V vs SHE.
chapters.trap: Do not treat the saturated calomel electrode as 0.00 V. Its potential is about +0.241 V vs SHE, and it changes with KCl concentration and temperature.
chapters.leave: pH-meter circuits and potentiometric titrations to 4.4; ion-selective electrodes other than glass to analytical chemistry.

chapters.idea: Potentiometry finds concentration from a near-zero-current cell EMF, and conductance finds electrolyte strength from the resistance of a solution.
chapters.depth: Potentiometric titration: reference electrode, indicator electrode, high-impedance voltmeter, endpoint from a sharp EMF jump; acid-base, redox and precipitation titrations. Conductance: specific conductance κ, cell constant l/A, resistance R, κ = (l/A)/R; molar conductance Λ_m = κ/c; equivalent conductance; strong and weak electrolytes; Kohlrausch law; conductometric titration curves. Some syllabi call this conductometry. Factors: concentration, temperature, nature of electrolyte.

figure.aria: Conductance falls linearly to a minimum at 25 mL of sodium hydroxide and then rises, the V-shape of a strong acid-strong base conductometric titration.

chapters.example: 25.0 mL of HCl is titrated conductometrically with 0.100 M NaOH. The conductance is minimum at 25.0 mL. Find the concentration of HCl. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol. HCl is 1:1, so moles HCl = 0.00250 mol. Concentration = 0.00250/0.0250 = 0.100 M.
chapters.trap: For every conductometric titration, do not take the minimum as the endpoint. For weak acid-strong base titrations the endpoint is the intersection of the straight-line parts, not always the minimum.
chapters.prereq: 4.1–4.3; basic resistance and conductivity from school physics.
chapters.leave: Activity coefficients and Debye–Hückel theory to physical chemistry; colorimetry and flame photometry to Unit 2 spectroscopy.

chapters.idea: A battery converts chemical energy to electrical energy; primary batteries are single-use, secondary batteries are rechargeable, and performance is judged by voltage, capacity, energy density and cycle life.
chapters.depth: Classification: primary (dry cell, alkaline, button cell) and secondary (lead-acid, Ni-Cd, Li-ion). Requirements: high energy density, stable voltage, low internal resistance, safety, low cost. Performance parameters: EMF, nominal voltage, capacity in Ah, C-rate, energy in Wh, energy density Wh kg⁻¹ and Wh L⁻¹, power density W kg⁻¹, self-discharge, cycle life, coulombic efficiency. Define capacity = current × time and energy = capacity × voltage. Some syllabi call this energy systems or battery technology.

figure.aria: A battery classification tree splits into primary cells such as dry and alkaline cells and secondary cells such as lead-acid, lithium-ion and nickel-cadmium.

chapters.example: A 12 V, 100 Ah lead-acid battery stores energy = 12 × 100 = 1200 Wh = 1.2 kWh. If it delivers 5 A for 10 h, charge used = 5 × 10 = 50 Ah, so depth of discharge = 50/100 = 50%.
chapters.trap: Ah is charge, not energy. Multiply ampere-hour capacity by voltage to get watt-hour energy; compare batteries by Wh kg⁻¹, not only by Ah.
chapters.leave: Lead-acid and Li-ion construction to 4.6; fuel cells and supercapacitors to 4.7.

chapters.idea: Lead-acid cells use Pb and PbO₂ in sulfuric acid, while Li-ion cells shuttle Li⁺ between graphite and a lithium metal oxide.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at construction-reaction depth. Lead-acid: Pb anode, PbO₂ cathode, dilute H₂SO₄, separator; discharge reactions Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ and PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; overall Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; about 2.1 V per cell, six cells for 12 V. Li-ion: LiCoO₂ or LiFePO₄ cathode, graphite anode, LiPF₆ in organic solvent, separator; Li⁺ intercalation and deintercalation; about 3.6–3.8 V per cell. Applications, advantages, disadvantages, overvoltage under load.

figure.title: Li-ion shuttle
figure.aria: On discharge lithium ions move from graphite anode through electrolyte to lithium cobalt oxide cathode while electrons pass through the load; charge reverses both flows.

chapters.example: A lead-acid cell has E = 2.10 V and the cell reaction transfers n = 2 electrons. Find ΔG per cell. ΔG = −nFE = −2 × 96485 × 2.10 = −405,237 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −405 kJ mol⁻¹.
chapters.trap: A lead-acid cell is about 2.1 V, not 12 V; a 12 V battery has six cells in series. Do not reverse the discharge reactions when writing recharge.
chapters.leave: Battery management systems, thermal-runaway modelling and recycling to specialized courses; fuel cells to 4.7.

chapters.idea: A fuel cell continuously converts fuel and oxidant to electricity, while a supercapacitor stores charge at a high-area surface or by fast surface redox.
chapters.depth: H₂-O₂ fuel cell: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O; overall H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O; E° = 1.23 V; efficiency and overpotential. Alkaline fuel cell (AFC) and proton-exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC): construction, working, advantages and disadvantages. Supercapacitors: electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC), pseudocapacitor, hybrid; C = Q/V, energy = ½CV², power = V²/(4R).

figure.aria: Layers of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell from hydrogen inlet through anode, electrolyte and cathode to water outlet.

chapters.example: A H₂-O₂ fuel cell operates at 1.00 V and delivers 0.500 A. Find power and energy in one hour. P = VI = 1.00 × 0.500 = 0.500 W. Energy = 0.500 W × 1 h = 0.500 Wh = 1800 J.
chapters.trap: A fuel cell is not a storage battery; it needs continuous fuel and oxidant. The thermodynamic 1.23 V is an upper limit, and the working voltage is lower because of activation and ohmic overpotential.
chapters.leave: Electroplating and electroless plating are metal-finishing topics outside these nine chapters; detailed electrocatalysis to advanced courses. Polymer paint chemistry to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Corrosion is electrochemical oxidation of a metal, the galvanic series ranks metals from active to noble, and moisture, pH, salts and area ratio control the rate.
chapters.depth: Dry and wet corrosion; electrochemical theory: anodic oxidation M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ and cathodic reduction of H⁺ or O₂. Rusting of iron: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; overall 2Fe + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2Fe(OH)₂ → hydrated Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Galvanic series from Mg, Zn, Al, Fe, Pb, Sn, Cu, Ag to Au. Difference from the standard electrode potential series. Factors: metal position, purity, passive film, moisture, pH, oxygen, chloride, temperature, stress, galvanic coupling and area ratio. Brief mention of uniform, galvanic, pitting, crevice and stress corrosion. Corrosion rate units such as mm year⁻¹.

figure.aria: A galvanic series stack from magnesium at the active top through zinc, aluminium, iron, lead, tin, copper and silver to gold at the noble bottom.

chapters.example: A steel plate of area 1.0 cm² is coupled to a copper plate of area 100 cm² in moist soil. The galvanic current is 10 mA. Find the anodic current density on steel. i = 10 mA / 1.0 cm² = 10 mA cm⁻². If the steel area were 100 cm², i = 10 mA / 100 cm² = 0.10 mA cm⁻².
chapters.trap: The galvanic series is not the same as the standard electrode potential series; it depends on the environment. A small anode joined to a large cathode corrodes much faster because the anodic current density is high.
chapters.leave: Detailed stress-corrosion cracking and metallurgy to materials engineering; control methods to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Corrosion is controlled by making the metal cathodic through cathodic protection, or by blocking its surface with coatings and inhibitors.
chapters.depth: Cathodic protection: sacrificial anode (Zn, Mg, Al) and impressed current with an inert anode and DC supply; protection potential and current requirement. Protective coatings: paint, varnish, enamel, metallic coatings such as galvanizing and tinning, electroplating, anodizing and conversion coatings. Inhibitors: anodic, cathodic and mixed. Design rules: avoid dissimilar metal joints, drain moisture, use inhibitors, maintain coatings.

figure.aria: A corrosion-control tree splits into cathodic protection by sacrificial anode or impressed current, and coatings such as paint, galvanizing and electroplating.

chapters.example: A steel tank of area 20 m² needs a protection current density of 10 mA m⁻². Find the total protection current. I = 10 mA m⁻² × 20 m² = 200 mA = 0.20 A.
chapters.trap: In cathodic protection the protected metal is the cathode; the sacrificial anode corrodes instead. Do not say the protected steel is the anode. Overprotection can cause hydrogen evolution and coating damage.
chapters.leave: Paint formulation and polymer chemistry to Unit 5; cathodic-protection design codes to civil and mechanical courses.
